title: Reducing the Shirom–Melamed Burnout Measure: Development and validation of nine-item and three-item short forms.
abstract: Job-related burnout is a central concern in occupational health psychology, yet practical constraints often limit the use of comprehensive measures. The 14-item Shirom-Melamed Burnout Measure (SMBM-14) is widely used and grounded in a three-facet symptom framework consisting of physical fatigue, cognitive weariness, and emotional exhaustion, but its length can be prohibitive in multiconstruct surveys and repeated-measures research. Across nine samples organized into four phases, we developed a nine-item short form (SMBM-9; three items per facet) and a three-item ultra-brief form (SMBM-3; one item per facet). Item reduction and structural results supported the intended three-facet structure of the SMBM-9 and the selection of a one-item-per-facet SMBM-3 composite. Internal consistency estimates were high for the SMBM-9 and lower, as expected, for the SMBM-3; both forms nevertheless showed high convergence with the SMBM-14 and established burnout measures. Across cross-sectional, panel, and daily diary designs, the brief forms reproduced the expected pattern of associations with work stressors, affective and distress-related constructs, and work and health outcomes, with the SMBM-9 tracking the SMBM-14 closely and the SMBM-3 showing modest differences consistent with its brevity. Additional longitudinal and within-person findings supported the usefulness of the brief forms in repeated-measures contexts, including high convergence with the SMBM-14 and similar relations with day-level work demands. These findings support the SMBM-9 as the preferred brief substitute when researchers want balanced coverage of the SMBM-14 facets, whereas the SMBM-3 is likely to be the more useful option when brevity itself is the primary objective and assessment space is severely constrained.
